book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook usually lists the three accords with their provisions side by side (Basel I: 8% CAR, risk weights; Basel II: three pillars; Basel III: buffers and ratios), often as a table. Here each accord is the answer to the failure of the one before: Basel I starts from a felt problem (borrowers default, losses are unexpected) and a question ('how much money?') that the risk table, the worked example and CAR answer in turn; Basel II enters because banks on one pillar still failed and two risks were uncovered; Basel III enters because banks on three pillars fell in 2008. The same picture of a bank on pillars is carried through all three and changed each time (one pillar, three pillars, iron middle pillar plus containers). Compared with part 1 (E26), which only named the risks, the institutions and the terms CAR, CRAR and RWA, this video teaches how the numbers work and what each accord added.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each accord is one piece, introduced by the failure the previous one left, and inside each accord every rule is a separate container or pillar added to the same bank picture.

opening.what: States that the video covers Basel 1, 2 and 3 in detail, then recalls the previous video (bank risks, BIS, BCBS, who made the accords) over the part-1 overview board.

moves.concept: recall: bank risks, BIS, BCBS, Basel I/II/III
moves.what: Today: Basel 1, 2 and 3 in detail.

moves.concept: recall: bank risks, BIS, BCBS, Basel I/II/III
moves.what: Previous video covered the risks in running a bank, BIS and its work, and BCBS, which formulated the accords.

moves.concept: credit risk and unexpected losses need a capital cushion
moves.what: 'Chaliye' start with Basel 1.

moves.concept: credit risk and unexpected losses need a capital cushion
moves.what: Basel 1 is about credit risk: a bank lends, many customers cannot repay, so banks suffer losses.

moves.concept: credit risk and unexpected losses need a capital cushion
moves.what: Why 'unexpected': nobody can say for sure how many customers will default.

moves.concept: credit risk and unexpected losses need a capital cushion
moves.what: So every bank should keep some money aside to absorb such losses.

moves.concept: credit risk and unexpected losses need a capital cushion
moves.what: 'But question ye hai': how much money is sufficient? This question drives the next three pieces.

moves.concept: risk categories and risk-weighted assets (RWA)
moves.what: Assets are categorised by risk into five categories with weights 0, 10, 20, 50 and 100%; the bank sorts its loans by this table and computes RWA (the opening words after 77 s are lost in a hidden transcript gap).

moves.concept: worked RWA example (1000 and 4000 Rs to 900 Rs)
moves.what: A bank has unsecured loans of 1000 and secured loans of 4000; at 50% and 10% the risks are 500 and 400; the sum, 900, is its RWA.

moves.concept: CAR / CRAR: capital as a percentage of RWA (8%, India 9%)
moves.what: The learner's objection voiced: why are we computing RWA when we wanted to know how much money is needed?

moves.concept: CAR / CRAR: capital as a percentage of RWA (8%, India 9%)
moves.what: Answer: if a bank keeps a percentage of its RWA safe, it can absorb future unexpected losses; that percentage is CAR, yaani capital adequacy ratio.

moves.concept: CAR / CRAR: capital as a percentage of RWA (8%, India 9%)
moves.what: BCBS suggested 8% in 1988; India adopted Basel 1 in 1999 (date worth checking), calls it CRAR, and keeps it 1% above the Basel value for stability.

moves.concept: CAR / CRAR: capital as a percentage of RWA (8%, India 9%)
moves.what: So now we know how much money a bank needs to absorb unexpected losses: this is the minimum capital requirement.

moves.concept: tier 1 vs tier 2 capital
moves.what: Minimum capital has two parts: tier 1 absorbs losses without the bank stopping its work, yaani no shutdown.

moves.concept: tier 1 vs tier 2 capital
moves.what: Tier 2 can also absorb losses, but it is not liquid; to raise it the bank may have to shut down.

moves.concept: tier 1 vs tier 2 capital
moves.what: Car analogy: a front guard takes small knocks and may break but the car and you are safe (tier 1); in a big accident the airbags open and save you (tier 2), but the car must be towed home.

moves.concept: tier 1 vs tier 2 capital
moves.what: 'I hope' the difference between tier 1 and tier 2 is now clear.

moves.concept: tier 1 vs tier 2 capital
moves.what: 'Ek baat hamesha dhyan rakhein': tier 1's loss-absorbing capacity is always more than tier 2's (a line to remember for the exam).

moves.concept: tier 1 as core capital and the components of each tier
moves.what: RBI judges a bank's strength by its tier 1 and tier 2; tier 1 is more reliable because it is liquid and usable at once, so it is the core measure, hence 'core capital'.

moves.concept: tier 1 as core capital and the components of each tier
moves.what: Tier 1 components: shareholders' equity and disclosed reserves (said to include SLR assets and liquid cash; needs checking).

moves.concept: tier 1 as core capital and the components of each tier
moves.what: Tier 2: undisclosed reserves, retained earnings (profit minus dividend) and fixed assets such as buildings and furniture (classification needs checking); an 11 s transcript gap falls inside this list.

moves.concept: tier 1 as core capital and the components of each tier
moves.what: So if a bank has to use tier 2 to cover losses, it almost has to close.

moves.concept: Basel I covers only credit risk
moves.what: Recap: Basel 1 had one focus, minimum capital of 8% of RWA in two tiers; it handles credit risk but not market or operational risk.

moves.concept: Basel II: three pillars and tier 1 at 4%
moves.what: Banks that had implemented Basel 1 were still failing, so in 2004 BCBS formulated Basel 2.

moves.concept: Basel II: three pillars and tier 1 at 4%
moves.what: A bank cannot be kept stable on one pillar; two more are needed: supervisory review and market discipline, which address market and operational risk.

moves.concept: Basel II: three pillars and tier 1 at 4%
moves.what: 'Ab question ye hai': what exactly are supervisory review and market discipline?

moves.concept: Basel II: three pillars and tier 1 at 4%
moves.what: Supervisory review looks at the bank's internal processes and systems, 'jabki' market discipline makes disclosure stricter for transparency.

moves.concept: Basel II: three pillars and tier 1 at 4%
moves.what: The existing pillar also changed: tier 1 must be at least 4% of RWA; whatever is above is tier 2.

moves.concept: Basel III: iron pillar and five containers
moves.what: Even on three pillars banks fell in the 2008 crisis, so the norms were upgraded to Basel 3 in 2010.

moves.concept: Basel III: iron pillar and five containers
moves.what: The middle pillar must be made of iron; 'kehne ka matlab', banks cannot depend on minimum capital alone and must keep money in many places for bad times.

moves.concept: Basel III: iron pillar and five containers
moves.what: The box, sack, piggy bank and briefcase on screen each stand for a Basel 3 term; each will be covered in turn.

moves.concept: Basel III capital numbers (9.5%, tier 3, tier 1 6%)
moves.what: Minimum capital raised to 9.5%, a tier 3 added to supplement tiers 1 and 2, tier 1 raised from 4.5% to 6% (all to be checked; the 4.5% contradicts the 4% given for Basel 2).

moves.concept: LCR: 30-day liquidity ratio
moves.what: LCR: the bank must hold enough high-quality liquid assets to survive at least 30 days in the worst case, as if shut in a box with a lid.

moves.concept: LCR: 30-day liquidity ratio
moves.what: 'Ek chhota sa confusion': we spoke of an amount, but LCR is a ratio, a percentage like CAR; its formula is HQLA over 30 days' net cash flows.

moves.concept: LCR: 30-day liquidity ratio
moves.what: If HQLA equals 30 days of net cash flows, LCR is 100%, which is what Basel 3 recommends.

moves.concept: NSFR: one-year stable funding
moves.what: 'Chaliye' now NSFR: how much money goes into this sack.

moves.concept: NSFR: one-year stable funding
moves.what: Each bank should fill a sack with enough money to get through a year of bad times.

moves.concept: NSFR: one-year stable funding
moves.what: Short bad times are handled by LCR; if they last longer, NSFR is needed; a year counts as medium term, enough time to bounce back.

moves.concept: CCCB: fill in good times, release in bad
moves.what: 'Chaliye' what to do with this piggy bank.

moves.concept: CCCB: fill in good times, release in bad
moves.what: Countercyclical capital buffer: put money into the piggy bank when times are good, break it and take the money out when times are bad.

moves.concept: CCCB: fill in good times, release in bad
moves.what: When to start filling and when to break it is decided not by the bank but by the country's central bank, RBI in India's case.

moves.concept: CCB: 2.5% of RWA
moves.what: The briefcase is the capital conservation buffer: 2.5% of RWA must be kept in it.

moves.concept: CCB: 2.5% of RWA
moves.what: Ultimately all this money is for the bank itself, in its bad times, when it needs it most.

moves.concept: India's ratios from the Financial Stability Report
moves.what: From the December 2022 Financial Stability Report: CRAR of all scheduled commercial banks 16%, also shown for public, private and foreign banks; 6.9% read as tier 1 (taken from a leverage-ratio chart).

moves.concept: India's ratios from the Financial Stability Report
moves.what: Both values are above the Basel recommendations; then a closing line and a playlist plug.

story_before_term.term: Basel II pillars (supervisory review, market discipline)

Car front guard (tier 1) vs airbags (tier 2); after the airbags, the car must be towed.

examples.what: A bank on pillars: one pillar (Basel 1), three pillars (Basel 2), iron middle pillar (Basel 3).
Box/jar, sack, piggy bank and briefcase standing for CAR, LCR, NSFR, CCCB and CCB.
Piggy bank filled in good times and broken in bad times.
Financial Stability Report December 2022 charts of CRAR and tier 1 leverage ratio by bank group.

closing.what: Ends on the FSR numbers with 'both values are above Basel's recommendation' and a one-line close plus playlist plug; the real recap is visual, the five containers sending arrows up to the bank at 781 s, and there is no exam link.

narration.density: About 25 terms (credit, market and operational risk, unexpected losses, asset categorisation, risk weight, RWA, CAR, CRAR, minimum capital requirement, tier 1, tier 2, tier 3, core capital, shareholders' equity, disclosed and undisclosed reserves, retained earnings, supervisory review, market discipline, LCR, HQLA, net cash flows, NSFR, CCCB, CCB, leverage ratio on screen) in about 830 s, about 1.8 per minute. The Basel I half is unhurried (one example, one analogy); the Basel III half drops a new acronym roughly every 40 s, held together by the container row. Right for UPSC; the second half is heavy for a first look.

talmel_summary: Picture and voice land together or with the picture about 1 s ahead in most tiles (11 together, 10 picture first, 3 voice first); the longer leads come where a container rises into the panel just before it is named. The picture carries meaning best where a metaphor changes on its word: the bank gains two pillars on 'pillars', the market and operational risk rows light up as Basel II is said to cover them, the middle pillar turns iron on 'iron', and all five containers send arrows to the bank on 'ultimately ... for the bank'. Weaker: the component lists and Basel III numbers are text that repeats the voice, some on-screen numbers are not spoken (9% CRAR) and some spoken ones are not shown (tier 1 4.5% to 6%, LCR 100%), the voice says 'break the piggy bank' and 'tow the car' with no matching action, and an imported leverage-ratio chart is read as tier 1 capital.

voice.notes: About 192 words per minute, faster than E57, conversational. Builds each step on a question ('but question ye hai', 'ab question ye hai ki aakhir...'), then answers it. Everyday Hindi nouns carry the metaphors (dabba, bori, gullak, briefcase, front guard, air bag) and are said with a light, playful tone. Numbers are read as digits with 'point' (9 point 5, 2 point 5, 6 point 9) and percentages are not stressed. 'Ek baat hamesha dhyan rakhein' marks the one exam-style takeaway. Recognition errors: 'Bank of International Settlements', 'RBIB', 'luhi' for lohe; one word stretched over 77-89 s hides about 11 s of speech, and there are gaps at 392.8-404.1 s and 462.7-466.5 s.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a bank's loan book: drags each new loan card (government bond, home loan, secured business loan, unsecured personal loan) into its risk category, then sets how much capital to put in the jar as a percentage of RWA.
game_ideas.process_happens: The RWA meter adds each loan times its weight (1000 at 50% shows 500); the jar shows the capital needed at 8% (or India's 9%); random default shocks hit, and the jar absorbs them or runs dry.
game_ideas.win: Survive a run of default shocks with the jar never empty while keeping as much money lent out as possible.
game_ideas.lose: Putting a risky loan in a low-risk row understates RWA, the jar is too small, and the first big default empties it: the bank fails and depositors queue outside.
game_ideas.concept: worked RWA example (1000 and 4000 Rs to 900 Rs)

game_ideas.player_does: Faces losses of different sizes and chooses which capital layer absorbs each: the front guard (tier 1) or the airbags (tier 2).
game_ideas.process_happens: Small losses absorbed by tier 1 leave the bank open and the guard is rebuilt; using tier 2 saves the depositors, but the bank's doors close and it is towed away.
game_ideas.win: Keep the bank open through a year of shocks by holding enough tier 1.
game_ideas.lose: Relying on tier 2 for a small loss shuts the bank needlessly; too little tier 1 forces tier 2 and closure.

game_ideas.player_does: Plays RBI across an economic cycle (boom, slowdown, crisis) and decides when banks must fill the piggy bank (CCCB) and when to let them break it.
game_ideas.process_happens: Filling in the boom slows runaway lending a little; breaking it in the crisis releases capital so banks keep lending; credit and failure meters move.
game_ideas.win: The piggy bank is full when the crisis arrives and released at once, so lending does not collapse.
game_ideas.lose: Filling it during the crisis squeezes credit when it is most needed; never filling it leaves nothing to release and banks fail.
game_ideas.concept: CCCB: fill in good times, release in bad

game_ideas.player_does: Builds the bank's support: places pillars (minimum capital, supervisory review, market discipline) and drops the five containers (CAR, LCR, NSFR, CCCB, CCB) under the right accord and time horizon.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each correct placement lights the risk it covers in the sidebar; LCR survives a 30-day storm, NSFR a 1-year one.
game_ideas.win: All three risks lit and every container on its accord and horizon.
game_ideas.lose: A bank on one pillar wobbles when a market shock arrives; LCR alone cannot get it through a year-long storm.
game_ideas.concept: Basel III: iron pillar and five containers

notes_questions.q: Risk weighted assets (RWA) kaise nikalte hain? 1000 unsecured aur 4000 secured loan ka example banaiye.
CAR (CRAR) kya hai? Basel I ne kitna kaha aur India mein kitna rakha gaya?
Tier 1 aur tier 2 capital mein kya fark hai? Car ke example se samjhaiye.
Tier 1 ko core capital kyon kehte hain?
Basel I, II aur III mein kya badla, aur har baar kyon badla?
Basel II ke teen pillars kaunse hain aur har pillar kis risk ke liye hai?
Basel III ke buffers (LCR, NSFR, CCCB, CCB): har ek kya karta hai aur kitne samay ke liye?
LCR ka formula kya hai aur 100% ka matlab kya hai?
Countercyclical capital buffer kab bhara jata hai, kab nikala jata hai, aur kaun decide karta hai?
Indian banks ka CRAR abhi kitna hai, aur Basel minimum se kaise compare karta hai?

checks_learned: A worked example must reach the answer to the question it was built for: RWA 900 at 8% gives 72 of capital; stopping at 900 leaves 'how much?' unanswered.
The same quantity must not get two values in one script (tier 1 minimum '4%' under Basel II, then 'previously 4.5%' under Basel III).
Every number on screen must be spoken (CRAR 9%) and every number spoken that matters must be shown (tier 1 4.5% to 6%, LCR 100%).

The label read out for a data chart must match the chart's own title (a 'Tier I leverage ratio' chart read as tier 1 capital); an achieved ratio from a report must not be called a requirement set by RBI.

Regulatory facts must be checked against the regulator's source before narration: Basel III tier 3, the 9.5% total, India's adoption year, what counts as disclosed reserves, where retained earnings and fixed assets belong, and the example's risk weights.
When the voice describes an action on a metaphor object (break the piggy bank, tow the car, close the jar's lid), the object must do it on screen on that word.
A metaphor set works when all objects appear together first, each is then lifted into a focus panel and returned, and they all come back together at the end (keep this pattern).
BIE's narration QA should flag a single word stretched over more than 3 s as a hidden gap (here 77-89 s) as well as normal silences.

teaching_best.why: 'How much money is enough?' is asked once and the jar labelled 'How much?' stays on screen until CAR answers it about 120 s later: one open question carries the whole Basel I half.
The learner's objection (why compute RWA when we wanted money?) is voiced right after the worked example and answered by CAR.
The car analogy (guard vs airbags, towed car) makes going-concern vs gone-concern capital obvious without either term.
One bank picture is carried across all three accords and changed each time (one pillar, three pillars, iron middle pillar), so the history of the accords is one growing picture.
Five everyday containers give five abstract buffers a shape and a place; the row stays on screen as an index while each is explained.
A likely confusion (LCR as an amount vs a ratio) is named and corrected before the formula.
LCR and NSFR are told apart by time horizon (30 days vs one year), the simplest way to keep them apart.

teaching_weak.why: The worked example ends at RWA = 900 and is never carried to the capital needed (8% of 900), the very number the question asked for.
Tier components are taught as lists, with several doubtful placements (SLR assets and cash as disclosed reserves, retained earnings and fixed assets in tier 2).
Basel III numbers (9.5%, a new tier 3, tier 1 from 4.5%) need checking and conflict with the earlier 4%.
The data close misreads a leverage-ratio chart as the tier 1 percentage and calls achieved ratios 'applied by RBI'.
About 11 s of narration is unrecoverable from the transcript while the risk table is introduced.
No spoken recap of the three accords and no exam link; only the visual arrows to the bank sum up Basel III.
